1.pericope_label: Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations
debates: Why this chapter follows the parable of the vine
Why a people of great knowledge must be told its own sins
How far the chapter is to be read as figure
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch explain the chapter as removing a false confidence, since a nation figured as a useless vine could still plead its election, and this shows Israel by nature no better than the nations around it

Henry observes that one prophet wrote from exile for the city and another from the city for the exiles, each sending what the other audience needed, consolation for the captives and conviction for those still at home

Clarke warns against taking the whole as figure, since there are many metaphors here and yet not everything is metaphorical, and where there was so much idolatry the vices that go with it must have been real
themes: A vine that pleads the vineyard it was planted in
Knowledge everywhere except about oneself
The glass of the law held up to a face that will not look
A cold self-knowledge wrapped in darkness

3.pericope_label: And say, Thus saith the Lord God unto Jerusalem; Thy birth and thy nativity is of the land of Canaan; thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite
debates: Why the covenant with Abraham is left out of account
When the birth of the nation is dated
What the word rendered to supple means
outliers: Calvin answers that the sentence describes only what the people were in themselves, since though God stood firm in his covenant they had by faithlessness cut themselves off, so that as far as they were concerned the promise was extinct and their adoption dead and buried

Gill dates the birth at the coming out of Egypt, Wesley at the call of Abraham from his idolatry, and Ellicott at the passage from the family of the patriarchs into bondage, adding that no other people ever became a nation despised and enslaved as this one was

Clarke sets beside the reproach a pagan parallel, the taunt that Aeneas was not born of a goddess but hewn from the entrails of a rock and suckled by tigers, and judges that the invective of the prophet exceeds it far
themes: A promise extinct on one side and firm on the other
A nation whose monuments were only then being read
A cord left uncut and a child left to perish
Swaddling that hinders the lungs it was meant to help

6.pericope_label: And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live
debates: Where the phrase about the blood belongs in the sentence
Whether one passing by is described or two
Why the figure of courtship is used at all
outliers: Ellicott holds that the phrase about the blood belongs with the speaking rather than the command, so that the word live was spoken while the child lay unclean, and notes that the Chaldee paraphrast took the other connection and drew a double reading from it, of the blood of circumcision and the blood of the passover

Calvin allows that the phrase might be read contemptuously, as if God grudged moving a hand where none of us willingly touches putrid gore, but takes it instead for the secret power by which the people were kept alive against nature
Calvin is uneasy with the courtship figure and explains it as accommodation, since God is not affected as men are and it is not according to his nature to love as young men do
themes: A word of life spoken over a child still in its blood
Love that can be accounted for by nothing in its object
A garment lappet that served as a counterpane
Increase that happened while they were still slaves

9.pericope_label: Then washed I thee with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with oil
debates: Whether the ornaments are to be read allegorically
What the jewel of the fourth verse was
How the language of the chapter is to be taken
outliers: Calvin refuses to allegorise the ornaments, saying such readers fruitlessly conjecture trifles that contradict one another, while Gill and Clarke both report the Targum reading that takes them of the law, the tabernacle service and the priestly vestments

Clarke supplies a key to the whole chapter, matching the infant to the low estate of the nation, the ornaments to its ordinances, the marriage to the covenant and the lovers who strip her to the nations she allied with, and advises the reader to forget the figures and look at the facts
Ellicott insists the sin was extraordinary and not called worse than others by mere hyperbole, since grace which does not elevate always reacts by directing to a lower depth
themes: Interpreters who contradict each other about the same jewel
A ring moved from the nose to the forehead by translators
Custom that sanctions the mode and prevents the abuse
Food given as though placed in the mouth by hand

14.pericope_label: But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by
debates: What the renown consisted in
How the kingdom came to trust in itself
Why idolatry is figured as harlotry
outliers: Ellicott explains the collapse as one of the most striking instances of providence in history, since the very means taken to make the kingdom a great empire became the instruments of its fall, the harem bringing in idolatry and the taxation supplying a pretext for revolt

Ellicott holds that the figure is not merely harlotry but indiscriminate harlotry, since the people never adopted one false god but worshipped the abominations of every nation that prevailed over them

Calvin traces pride to immodesty, since a modest man would be restrained from all insolence, and observes that whatever a man excels in he arrogates more to himself than he ought, riches turning to pomp and ability to cunning
themes: Fame held by gift and mistaken for merit
Means of greatness that became instruments of ruin
An empire that fell apart like a rope of sand
A snare men seldom recover themselves out of

16.pericope_label: And of thy garments thou didst take, and deckedst thy high places with divers colours, and playedst the harlot thereupon
debates: What the images of men were
What the closing clause of the first verse means
Why the misuse of the gifts is worse than the idolatry itself
outliers: Clarke identifies the images with the emblems carried in certain ancient fertility processions, citing Herodotus, and Wesley allows the same cautiously; Keil and Delitzsch reject that reading outright, saying it is impossible to find the slightest trace of such worship among the Israelites and that the arguments for it had already been answered

Ellicott notes that coloured tapestry adorned places of worship universally in antiquity and was a feature of the tabernacle itself, so that what is censured is the perversion of a thing meant for the glory of God

Ellicott draws the principle that the heart of the charge is that the gifts came from God and were given to another, which must for ever remain true of any talent turned to a use other than his service
themes: A high place pitched where it will be seen
A passion fed on the picture of its object
Incense of his own herbs burnt to another
Luxuries consumed badly by those who did not grow them

20.pericope_label: Moreover thou hast taken thy sons and thy daughters, whom thou hast borne unto me, and these hast thou sacrificed unto them to be devoured
debates: Whether passing through the fire always means death
In what sense the children were the children of God
Where the first clause of the later verse belongs
outliers: Clarke and Calvin both cite the same classical account of people leaping over fires for purification, Clarke inferring that the phrase does not always mean the child was consumed, and Calvin that there were two kinds of offering

Calvin distinguishes a general election of the whole family of Abraham, sealed by circumcision, from a secret election of those taken out of that multitude, so that the men spoken of here were strangers in the one sense and his people in the other
Calvin rejects the reading that takes the first clause separately as a threat that their nakedness would be laid bare again, calling it forced, and joins it to what follows
themes: A father affection extinguished and a man made a monster
Obedience with a command and madness without one
A high place at every corner as an open boast
Neighbours who hated her and were ashamed of her

24.pericope_label: That thou hast also built unto thee an eminent place, and hast made thee an high place in every street
debates: What the eminent place was
Whether the Assyrian verse charges idolatry or treaty
What the land of Canaan unto Chaldea means
Where the diminished ordinary points
outliers: Calvin claims the chapter charges two different kinds of fornication, idolatry and forbidden treaties, and says the interpreters do not observe this
Clarke traces the word through the Latin, an old manuscript Bible, Coverdale and Diodati, deriving the modern brothel from an Italian word
Ellicott prefers the sense of traffic for Canaan, so that the idolatries travelled outward along her commerce
Calvin sets aside the rendering of Jerome, who took the word for a statute and explained it of the law
themes: A brothel, an altar, a pit and arches for one word
Fools grow wise only by the rod
The heathen repelled by the unworthiness of professed followers
Two powers in deadly hostility courted at once

30.pericope_label: How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman
debates: Whether a dissolute heart and an imperious woman can be charged together
How the word rendered weak should be taken
Whether she is an adulteress at home or one who deserts her house
outliers: Calvin answers the apparent contradiction by holding both faults at once, that despisers of God flow away like water and yet are hard as rocks
Calvin draws from the high places a rule that worship is not to be estimated by our own perception, since obedience is preferred to all sacrifices
Ellicott reads the verse politically, both kingdoms buying foreign interference at a heavy price when their position should have made their friendship worth courting
Gill distinguishes idolatry in a people married to the Lord as adultery from the same sin among the Gentiles as simple fornication
themes: A heart that flows like water and stands like rock
The harlot who pays instead of being paid
A farthing grudged and guineas thrown away
A mouth stopped before the equity of the sentence

36.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thy filthiness was poured out, and thy nakedness discovered through thy whoredoms with thy lovers
debates: Whether the opening word means money or filth
Whether the fury resting means mitigation or satiety
Whether the stones are thrown by engines of war
Whether the last clause should be read in the first person
outliers: Ellicott explains the two modes of execution from the law, stoning for an individual and the sword for an apostate city, and grants that pairing them strains the consistency of the allegory
Calvin turns the doubled charge against the plea of good intention, since they pleaded zeal and God branded wickedness upon them
Clarke reads the quiet as complete abandonment, and calls the ceasing of reproof the severest judgment of all
Ellicott prefers the first person against the Masoretic pointing, so that the clause says it would be wrong to leave such sin unpunished
themes: Brass named contemptuously where gold or silver was usual
Blood given to idols and blood given back to drink
Houses burnt so that no successors could come
A husband whose anger ends in the public punishment

44.pericope_label: Behold, every one that useth proverbs shall use this proverb against thee, saying, As is the mother, so is her daughter
debates: Whether elder and younger mean age or size
What Sodom stands for here
How the sisters can be said to have loathed husbands
Whether the denial of walking in their ways exempts or compares
outliers: Calvin explains the resemblance of daughters to mothers by education rather than nature, since a woman of perverse inclination thinks a stigma attaches to her if her daughter is better
Clarke doubts the plain identification and supposes Sodom here means those who dwelt beyond Jordan, since the city existed before Jerusalem had a name
Ellicott answers the difficulty about husbands by holding that the heathen sisters had gone astray from a primeval revelation
Calvin finds a method in the order of the charges, the incredible comparison proposed first so that the greater one would be heard
themes: Judging ourselves good enough by comparison with the passable
Few sober daughters brought up by drunkards
Facing the east, so that the north is the left hand
Not walking in their ways because they were left behind

48.pericope_label: As I live, saith the Lord GOD, Sodom thy sister hath not done, she nor her daughters, as thou hast done, thou and thy daughters
debates: How a people with true worship could be worse than one without
Whether the sin listed here is the one the city is remembered for
How justifying the sisters can stand with judging them
Whether the later promise contradicts the doom just pronounced
outliers: Calvin divides pride into two horns, claiming what belongs to God and refusing to acknowledge ones own vices
Ellicott notes that the crimes always associated with that name are not mentioned, the sin specified being the failure to strengthen the hand of the poor and needy
Clarke connects the comparative justified with the man who went down to his house justified rather than the other
Ellicott rejects the attempts of commentators to read the declaration of impossibility as a covert promise
themes: An oath sworn by his own life because there is no greater
Fulness of bread and abundance of idleness
The flower of the people kept safe and sound
Growing hot against others as if that covered ones own crimes

53.pericope_label: When I shall bring again their captivity, the captivity of Sodom and her daughters, and the captivity of Samaria and her daughters
debates: Whether the turn of captivity is a promise or a denial
Whether the restoration is to be taken literally
Why the destruction of Sodom was never spoken of
Whose reproach the last verse means
outliers: Ellicott holds that conditioning restoration on an impossible thing is the strongest possible way of denying it
Calvin answers the promises of return elsewhere by distinguishing the whole body of the nation from the remnant, a hidden seed preserved as in a sepulchre
Calvin rejects the reading that makes the Sodomites here mean the Moabites and Ammonites, the descendants of Lot
Ellicott doubts the view that refers the reproach to her own exultation at the fall of her neighbours
themes: A city with no descendants left to restore
Consolation in perishing among a great multitude
A lake of sulphur set in the paradise of God
Sin known only by being discovered in its punishment

58.pericope_label: Thou hast borne thy lewdness and thine abominations, saith the LORD
debates: Whether God is freed from the covenant by their breach of it
When the days of youth were
Whether the covenant promised is new or the old renewed
Whether the earlier words about the sisters returning are a promise
outliers: Calvin answers the appeal to the covenant by the rule that a man deceived is no longer bound to a perfidious breaker, since there is no covenant when either party declines it
Gill dates the covenant remembered to Sinai and Clarke to Abraham, while Wesley holds both together
Ellicott points to the contrast between the covenant God calls his own and the one he calls theirs in the next verse
Calvin makes shame the condition of receiving grace, since if we wish our sins buried before God we must remember them ourselves
themes: Enormities weighed and found heavier than the punishment
No covenant where either party declines it
Mercy remembered after the denunciation
Sure mercies because they are covenant mercies

62.pericope_label: And I will establish my covenant with thee; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD
debates: How far the new covenant continues the old
What the word rendered pacified means
Whether the promise is made to the nation or to a remnant
outliers: Ellicott makes the old covenant merge in the new, the less perfect having necessarily prepared the way for the perfect
Calvin holds that the new covenant takes its origin from the old, so that those reconciled are grafted into the ancient body and made sons of Abraham
Ellicott corrects pacified to pardoned, the original being the technical word in the law for covering up sins
Clarke directs the reader back to his note on the thirteenth verse as the key to the metaphors of the whole chapter
themes: A covenant that survives the perfidy of the people
A people created in order to praise
Sins put out of sight because looking at them wounds
Shame and comfort increasing together
